The Magnus expansion in relativistic quantum field theory
and Pablo Vives Matasan

Abstract
We investigate the Magnus expansion of the N N -operator in relativistic quantum field theory, which is related to the S S -matrix via S = e i ​ N S=e^{iN} . We develop direct methods to compute matrix elements of the N N -operator, which we refer to as Magnus amplitudes, bypassing scattering amplitudes entirely. At tree level, Magnus amplitudes are expressed in terms of retarded and advanced propagators, with each diagram weighted by factors that we identify as Murua coefficients. At loop level this structure is augmented by the Hadamard cut function, and we establish remarkable relations between loop- and tree-level Magnus amplitudes. Among these, we find that n n -point one-loop Magnus amplitudes are entirely determined by phase-space integrals of forward limits of ( n + 2 ) (n{+}2) -point tree-level amplitudes, and hence related to Murua coefficients, and we generalise this to a class of higher-loop contributions. Furthermore, in the case of heavy particles interacting via massless mediators, we conjecture that Magnus diagrams that contribute to the classical limit are always given by forward limits of trees, and we show this explicitly in a one-loop example. We derive these results studying theories of scalar fields with cubic interactions, but our methods are applicable to general theories as well as to integral functions appearing in gravitational-wave computations. Given that Magnus amplitudes are free of hyper-classical terms, and the known relations between Magnus amplitudes and the radial action, our results lay the groundwork for systematic and efficient calculations of classical observables from quantum field theory.



QMUL-PH-25-27

1
Introduction

The
S
-matrix is the cornerstone of quantum field theory calculations, encoding all physical scattering amplitudes from which observable quantities can be computed. Since the development of perturbation theory, physicists have predominantly relied on the Dyson series
[
1
]
to compute
S
-matrix elements – a time-honoured approach that expands the time evolution operator as an infinite sum of time-ordered products of interaction Hamiltonians. However, an alternative formulation exists that has remained relatively unexplored in the context of relativistic quantum field theory: the Magnus expansion

[
2
]
.

The Magnus expansion takes a different approach to the time evolution operator by writing it in exponential form,
U(t,t_{0})=e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}N(t,t_{0})}
, and then finding
N(t,t_{0})
as a perturbative series – the Magnus expansion.
Applied to the

S
-matrix this yields

S{=}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}N}
, with
N
determined order by order through the Magnus expansion. There are two important advantages of this approach. First, by writing the evolution operator or the
S
-matrix as exponentials, unitarity is manifest at every order, since

N(t,t_{0})
and
N
are hermitian at any finite order by construction.
1
1

1

The
S
-matrix computed using standard Feynman rules is only unitary when all orders of perturbation theory are included. In contrast, the Magnus expansion naturally incorporates resummations, ensuring that the
S
-matrix remains unitary at every finite order in perturbation theory.

Second, the exponential representation is particularly well suited when the interaction Hamiltonian is not small, such as in collision processes relevant for chemical physics
[
3
]
.

The
S
-matrix can be seen as the limit of a sequence of infinitesimal steps of the form
e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}H_{I}(t)\Delta t}
, where
H_{I}(t)
is the interaction Hamiltonian. In this sense, the evolution operator in its exponential form itself can be viewed as a “continuous” generalisation of the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula
[
3
]
. It is therefore not surprising that
the
N
-operator is constructed from nested commutators of the interaction Hamiltonian, in stark contrast to the time-ordered products appearing in the Dyson series.
For example, at second order in perturbation theory, the Dyson series for the
S
-matrix contains the time-ordered product of two Hamiltonians,
T\{H_{I}(t_{1})H_{I}(t_{2})\}
, while the Magnus expansion for the
N
-operator features terms such as

\theta(t_{1}-t_{2})[H_{I}(t_{1}),H_{I}(t_{2})]
, which in turn give rise to causal propagators.

This reorganisation of the perturbative series has profound consequences for its mathematical structure and physical implications.
In particular, at the
n^{\rm th}
order the relevant term scales as
[H_{I}(t_{1}),[H_{I}(t_{2}),[\ldots,[H_{I}(t_{n-1}),H_{I}(t_{n})]\ldots]]]/\hbar^{n}\!\sim\!\mathcal{O}(1/\hbar)
if we assume that
[H_{I}(t_{i}),H_{I}(t_{i+1})]\sim\hbar
, and hence such a contribution is classical.
Crucially, this structure ensures that no hyper-classical terms
2
2

2

These are terms that diverge in the classical
\hbar\to 0
limit which can appear in
S
-matrix elements, but cancel out when one computes classical observables.

appear at any order in the expansion of the
N
-operator (and of its matrix elements), as discussed in
[
4
,
5
,
6
]
, and
taking the classical limit becomes a simple task.

While Magnus’s original work focused on linear differential equations, its application to quantum mechanics was recognised early on
[
7
,
3
]
. The expansion was quickly adopted in atomic and molecular physics, and became especially valuable in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, where it provided the foundation for Average Hamiltonian Theory in analysing time-dependent spin dynamics
[
8
,
9
,
10
]
.
In condensed matter physics, the Magnus expansion became an important tool for understanding driven quantum systems, particularly in the context of Floquet theory and periodically driven Hamiltonians

[
11
,
12
,
13
,
14
]
. Mathematicians have also long been fascinated by the Magnus expansion, initially motivated by its connection to the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula and Lie group theory mentioned earlier, see e.g.
[
15
]
, with more recent applications extending to the computation of Feynman integrals
3
3

3

A comprehensive treatment of the Magnus expansion and its applications, with extensive references, is given in
[
16
]
, while a more pedagogical exposition is provided in
[
17
]
.

[
18
]
.

Recent work
[
6
,
19
]
has demonstrated that the Magnus expansion provides a natural framework for computing the radial action in worldline quantum field theory (WQFT)
[
20
]

– a quantity that encodes classical scattering data without quantum corrections, and which is also free of hyper-classical contributions.
This development represents a significant advance in extracting classical physics from quantum calculations.
The key technical innovation in the approach of
[
6
]
is a representation of the Magnus expansion in terms of “directed trees”, diagrams where retarded and advanced propagators are shown as arrows. Each tree diagram
\tau
is weighted by a combinatorial factor
\omega(\tau)
that can be computed algorithmically using an extension of a formula by Murua
[
21
]
, thus
providing diagrammatic rules for matrix elements at tree level in the WQFT. For this reason, we refer to
\omega(\tau)
as Murua coefficients in the rest of this work.

The radial action
I_{r}(J)=\int\!dr\,p_{r}
is a central object in classical gravitational scattering, as
it encodes the complete information about classical trajectories, both for bound and unbound orbits. In particular, the scattering angle can then be obtained as
\chi=-\partial I_{r}/\partial J
,
and other observables such as the periastron advance for bound orbits can also be derived from it
[
22
]
.
The connection between scattering amplitudes and the radial action was introduced in
[
23
]
, schematically written as

M({\vec{q}})=\int_{J}\big(e^{I_{r}(J)}-1\big)
, where
M
is the four-point (elastic) amplitude and
{\vec{q}}
is the transferred momentum.
It is also believed that the radial action describing the classical dynamics of spinless black holes or neutron stars
can be extracted from the four-point matrix element of the
N
-operator
[
4
]
.
In that paper, the scattering angle of two spinless black holes was computed to the third Post-Minkowskian (PM) order precisely from the four-point
N
-matrix element (see also
[
24
]
for a derivation from the closely related HEFT expansion). The use of the
N
operator was further explored in
[
5
]
, where the momentum kick (and hence the scattering angle) was obtained at fourth PM order. The relation between the radial action and other, well-known exponential representations of classical scattering (e.g. the eikonal, see the review
[
25
]
and references therein) was explored recently in
[
26
,
27
]
.
The
N
-operator is also a key ingredient in the recently developed Dirac bracket formalism
[
28
,
29
,
30
,
6
,
31
]
, where observables are derived by taking iterated brackets of
N
-matrix elements. Indeed, at least in the conservative sector of two-to-two scattering, iterated quantum commutators like those described above become Dirac brackets in the classical limit.

The calculations of
[
4
,
5
]
were performed by relating
N
-matrix elements (which we will
refer to as Magnus amplitudes) to
S
-matrix elements, that is ordinary scattering amplitudes, which are computed with the usual Feynman
i\epsilon
prescription.
As mentioned earlier,
N
-matrix elements are free of hyper-classical terms; furthermore the
N
-matrix is hermitian and this implies that
N
-matrix elements of real scalars are real.
However, by computing them via scattering amplitudes, one is forced to compute such hyper-classical terms, even though ultimately they cancel. The HEFT approach of
[
24
]
partially improves on this by working directly with classical quantities and thus
avoiding the computation and the need to explicitly cancel hyper-classical terms, at least up to two loops. Yet this approach leads to matrix elements which contain an imaginary, divergent part and hence are not immediately (though very closely) related to Magnus amplitudes and the radial action (up to two loops, the radial action can be identified with the real part of the four-point HEFT matrix element).

The preceding discussion motivates the main goal of this paper: the direct computation of Magnus amplitudes completely bypassing scattering amplitudes, in a relativistic quantum field theory setting. While ultimately, in a gravitational-wave context, one may be interested in just computing classical terms, we will keep our discussion general. Unlike
[
6
]
, we work in a quantum field theory, specifically that of a real scalar field with a
\phi^{3}
coupling. This is a toy model that nevertheless captures all the essential features of a general calculation, and the main lessons can then be exported to other theories. Furthermore, many integral functions in a theory with a single mass (or no mass) can be represented within
\phi^{3}
theory. Therefore one can imagine performing a calculation in a general quantum field theory, reducing it to a set of integrals that correspond to diagrams in our
\phi^{3}
theory, which can then be evaluated with the prescriptions developed in this paper.

Generally speaking, these prescriptions correspond to replacing Feynman propagators with advanced, retarded or cut propagators, and weighting each diagram with specific factors. Our calculations will reveal that, both at tree level and one loop (and partially at higher loops), these factors are precisely the Murua coefficients. Once this is established, one may compute them either directly or, much more economically, by applying Murua’s formula. Importantly, as we shall see, all the
\theta
-functions that appear in (and are a key feature of) the Magnus expansion
(see e.g. (
2.9
)) recombine to yield advanced and retarded propagators, as expected from Lorentz invariance.

We will also find that
N
-matrix elements at different loop orders are tightly interconnected (in a way illustrated in Figure
1
). At one loop this relation takes on an especially simple and beautiful form: the
n
-point one-loop Magnus amplitudes are completely determined by the phase-space integral of forward limits of the corresponding
(n+2)
-point tree-level Magnus amplitudes. Interestingly, this statement can be generalised to higher loops, as we will study in the following sections.
4
4

4

The idea of obtaining loops from integrated trees appears in several contexts. The Feynman tree theorem provides an early example
[
32
,
33
]
, with modern applications related to the tree theorem appearing in
[
34
,
35
]
, in the loop–tree duality approach of
[
36
,
37
]
, and in the
Q
-cuts of
[
38
]
.

The relations described above were found using an improved set of Wick contractions specialised to the Magnus expansion. We have implemented these Wick contractions in code, obtaining explicit results for (unintegrated) Magnus amplitudes in
\phi^{3}
theory up to six vertices and four loops, and seven vertices and two loops. These results are provided in the companion repository
Magnus expansion in QFT
.

Up to this point the discussion has concerned the full quantum theory, but for applications to gravity and the radial action it is important to focus on the classical limit. Based on a simple example, we put forward a conjecture directly relating particular cut diagrams in the field theory to diagrams in the WQFT.

The Magnus expansion offers then a powerful framework for studying perturbative quantum field theory, making unitarity manifest and providing direct access to classical observables. By developing explicit prescriptions and illustrating them in a simple yet representative scalar model, we aim to clarify the underlying structure of Magnus amplitudes at loop level and its connection to Murua’s work, at the same time establishing practical tools for future applications, particularly to gravitational physics.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. In the next section we give a brief review of the Dyson and Magnus expansions, contrasting the main characteristics of the two: while the first involves time-ordered products of the Hamiltonian, the second involves nested commutators of the same quantity. We will also present a new closed formula for the
n^{\rm th}
order term in the Magnus expansion, as an alternative to the known Chen-Strichartz formula. Section
3
summarises the cast of characters that will appear in what will follow: commutation functions, propagators and the Hadamard function. We then begin to explore Magnus amplitudes perturbatively, first at tree level
in Section
4
and then at one loop in Section
5
. We will compute Magnus amplitudes explicitly, via Wick contractions, up to six (three) points at tree level (one loop), from which we will learn two key lessons: that each diagram is weighted with particular factors, which we will later associate to
Murua coefficients; and that one-loop coefficients are related to tree-level ones. After gaining this insight, in Section
6
we show how at tree level these coefficients can be obtained in a much simpler way from the Murua formula. We also establish a tree/one-loop correspondence: as mentioned earlier each one-loop diagram contains one cut propagator, and its coefficient is half the Murua coefficient of the tree-level diagram obtained by deleting the cut line (see (
6.14
)).
This fact reflects a general correspondence between loops and trees, which we explore in Section
7
.
We establish this relation using a set of simplified Wick-contraction rules that we have developed, and summarise it in Figure
1
.
The main lesson is that Magnus amplitudes with
L+\ell
loops and
C+\ell
cuts can be obtained from
\ell
forward limits of Magnus amplitudes with
L
loops and
C
cuts. In particular, this means all amplitudes with
\ell
loops and
\ell
cuts can be obtained from
\ell
forward limits of tree-level amplitudes; we believe these contain all classical contributions and present evidence for this in Section
8
, where we also show in a simple example the cancellation of hyper-classical terms.
We conclude in Section
9
by summarising our results and outlining possible directions for future work.
A few Appendices complete the paper. In particular Appendix
A
summarises all the main diagrammatic properties of the Magnus expansion, while the remaining appendices
expand on some technical aspects of our work.

2
Dyson and Magnus: old and new

2.1
Review of the Dyson and Magnus expansions

We begin by recalling that the evolution of a state
|t\rangle
in the interaction picture is governed by the equation (setting
\hbar=1
from now on)

i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}|t\rangle=H_{I}(t)|t\rangle\,.

(2.1)

Here the Hamiltonian is
H\coloneq H_{0}+V
, where

H_{I}(t)
is the interaction Hamiltonian time-evolved with the free Hamiltonian
H_{0}
, that is
H_{I}(t)\coloneq e^{iH_{0}t}Ve^{-iH_{0}t}
. By writing the states in terms of the time-evolution operator,
|t\rangle=U(t,t_{0})|t_{0}\rangle
, we can recast (
2.1
) as an operator differential equation,

i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}U(t,t_{0})=H_{I}(t)U(t,t_{0})\,.

(2.2)

This can be solved iteratively to yield the Dyson series
[
1
]
,

\displaystyle U(t,t_{0})

\displaystyle=1+(-i)\int_{t_{0}}^{t}dt_{1}\ H_{I}(t_{1})+(-i)^{2}\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}dt_{1}dt_{2}\ H_{I}(t_{1})H_{I}(t_{2})+\cdots

\displaystyle=1+(-i)\int_{[t_{0},t]}dt_{1}\ H_{I}(t_{1})+\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2!}\int_{[t_{0},t]^{2}}dt_{1}dt_{2}\ T\big\{H_{I}(t_{1})H_{I}(t_{2})\big\}+\cdots

\displaystyle=1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-i)^{n}}{n!}\int_{[t_{0},t]^{n}}dt_{1}\cdots dt_{n}\ T\big\{H_{I}(t_{1})\cdots H_{I}(t_{n})\big\}\,.

(2.3)

Evaluating this from
t_{0}=-\infty
to
t=\infty
computes the
S
-matrix

\displaystyle S:=U(+\infty,-\infty)\,,

(2.4)

which is then expanded as

\displaystyle S

\displaystyle=1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-i)^{n}}{n!}\int dx_{1}\cdots dx_{n}\ T\big\{\mathcal{H}_{I}(x_{1})\cdots\mathcal{H}_{I}(x_{n})\big\}\,,

(2.5)

with
H_{I}(t)\coloneq\int\!d^{3}x\,\mathcal{H}_{I}(x)
.

An alternative way to solve (
2.2
) is to instead write the time evolution operator itself in exponential form
[
2
]
,

U(t,t_{0}):=e^{iN(t_{,}t_{0})}\,,

(2.6)

and solve for the operator
N(t,t_{0})
. The derivation of this solution is more involved, with a general form given by Magnus
[
2
]
. The first few terms of this Magnus series are

\displaystyle iN^{(1)}(t,t_{0})

\displaystyle=-i\int_{[t_{0},t]}dt_{1}\ H_{1}\,,

(2.7a)

\displaystyle iN^{(2)}(t,t_{0})

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}\int_{[t_{0},t]^{2}}dt_{1}dt_{2}\ \theta_{12}\ [H_{1},H_{2}]\,,

(2.7b)

\displaystyle iN^{(3)}(t,t_{0})

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{3}}{6}\int_{[t_{0},t]^{3}}dt_{1}dt_{2}dt_{3}\ \theta_{12}\theta_{23}\,\left([H_{1},[H_{2},H_{3}]]+[H_{3},[H_{2},H_{1}]]\right)

(2.7c)

\displaystyle iN^{(4)}(t,t_{0})

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{4}}{12}\int_{[t_{0},t]^{4}}dt_{1}dt_{2}dt_{3}dt_{4}\ \theta_{12}\theta_{23}\theta_{34}\big([H_{1},[H_{2},[H_{3},H_{4}]]]

(2.7d)

\displaystyle+[H_{4},[H_{3},[H_{1},H_{2}]]]+[H_{2},[H_{3},[H_{4},H_{1}]]]+[H_{1},[H_{4},[H_{3},H_{2}]]]\big)\,,

where we have written
H_{i}:=H_{I}(t_{i})
and
\theta_{ij}:=\theta(t_{i}-t_{j})
for compactness.
We can write similar formulae for the
S
-matrix. Defining

\displaystyle S\coloneq e^{iN}=e^{iN(+\infty,-\infty)}\,,

(2.8)

we have, for the first few orders,

\displaystyle iN^{(1)}

\displaystyle=-i\int\!d^{4}x_{1}\ \mathcal{H}_{1}\,,

(2.9a)

\displaystyle iN^{(2)}

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\ \theta_{12}\ [\mathcal{H}_{1},\mathcal{H}_{2}]\,,

(2.9b)

\displaystyle iN^{(3)}

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{3}}{6}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}\ \theta_{12}\theta_{23}\,\left([\mathcal{H}_{1},[\mathcal{H}_{2},\mathcal{H}_{3}]]+[\mathcal{H}_{3},[\mathcal{H}_{2},\mathcal{H}_{1}]]\right)\,

(2.9c)

\displaystyle iN^{(4)}

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{4}}{12}\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}d^{4}x_{4}\ \theta_{12}\theta_{23}\theta_{34}\big([\mathcal{H}_{1},[\mathcal{H}_{2},[\mathcal{H}_{3},\mathcal{H}_{4}]]]

(2.9d)

\displaystyle+[\mathcal{H}_{4},[\mathcal{H}_{3},[\mathcal{H}_{1},\mathcal{H}_{2}]]]+[\mathcal{H}_{2},[\mathcal{H}_{3},[\mathcal{H}_{4},\mathcal{H}_{1}]]]+[\mathcal{H}_{1},[\mathcal{H}_{4},[\mathcal{H}_{3},\mathcal{H}_{2}]]]\big)\,.

At low perturbative orders, expressions involving a small number of nested commutators are known and have been reproduced in the formulae above. However, there is no general formula which provides compact expressions for any
n
, though they can in principle be produced algorithmically
[
39
]
. If we drop the minimality requirement, there do exist general closed form expressions for any
n
. One of these, which we will make use of later, is known as the Chen-Strichartz (CS) formula
[
40
]
, and reads

\displaystyle iN=\sum_{n\geq 1}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\frac{(-1)^{d_{\sigma}}}{n^{2}\binom{n-1}{d_{\sigma}}}\int

\displaystyle\!d^{4}x_{1}\cdots d^{4}x_{n}\ \theta_{12}\theta_{23}\cdots\theta_{n-1\,n}

(2.10)

\displaystyle\Big[\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(1)},\big[\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(2)},\cdots[\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(n-1)},\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(n)}]\cdots\big]\Big]\,.

Here the natural number
d_{\sigma}=|D_{\sigma}|
is the descent number of the permutation
\sigma
, and
D_{\sigma}
its descent set:

D_{\sigma}=\big\{i\ |\ \sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1),1\leq i<n\big\}\,.

(2.11)

The descent set labels at which points in the permutation two consecutive numbers are descending, and the descent number just counts the number of such occurrences. For example, for the set
\{1,2,3,4\}
,

D_{4213}=\{1,2\}\,,\qquad D_{3124}=\{1\}\,,\qquad D_{4321}=\{1,2,3\}\,,\qquad D_{2413}=\{2\}\,,

(2.12)

with

d_{4213}=2\,,\qquad d_{3124}=1\,,\qquad d_{4321}=3\,,\qquad d_{2413}=1\ .

(2.13)

The CS formula contains
n!
terms. There are quick ways to reduce the number of terms contributing to a certain order in the Magnus expansion, such as flipping the innermost commutator on half of the terms, but this spoils the structure of (
2.10
) as doing so mixes permutations of different descent number. In Section
2.2
, we will be able to present an alternative formula for the Magnus expansion where the sum is not over permutations but over “descent sets”, which
contains only
2^{n-1}
terms.

We also notice that, due to Jacobi relations, the nested commutators form an overcomplete basis. In particular one can recast (
2.10
) as
[
41
,
42
]

\displaystyle iN=\sum_{n\geq 1}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n-1}}\frac{(-1)^{d_{\sigma}}}{n\binom{n-1}{d_{\sigma}}}\int

\displaystyle\!d^{4}x_{1}\cdots d^{4}x_{n}\ \theta_{12}\theta_{23}\cdots\theta_{n-1\,n}

(2.14)

\displaystyle\Big[\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(1)},\big[\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(2)},\cdots[\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(n-1)},\mathcal{H}_{n}]\cdots\big]\Big]\,,

where one Hamiltonian is inserted at a fixed point
n
, which is reminiscent of the work of
[
43
]
.

2.2
A new formula for the Magnus expansion

In this section we present an alternative formula (
2.20
) for the Magnus expansion, requiring the reorganisation of the sum over permutations present in the Chen-Strichartz formula (
2.10
). Our formula contains
2^{n-1}
terms at order
n
in perturbation theory, hence it presents a computational advantage compared to the
n!
scaling of the CS formula.

Consider the term in the CS formula (
2.10
) at a fixed order
n
in perturbation theory,
iN^{(n)}
. We can group all the permutations in
S_{n}
appearing in the sum by their descent set, defined in (
2.11
). Suppose we label the set of all permutations with descent set
D
by
S_{n}^{D}
. Consider similarly dividing the sum in
iN^{(n)}
into chunks of constant descent set,

\displaystyle iN^{(n)}=

\displaystyle\sum_{D}\frac{(-1)^{|D|}}{n^{2}\binom{n-1}{|D|}}\sum_{\sigma\in S^{D}_{n}}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}\cdots d^{4}x_{n}\ \theta_{12}\theta_{23}\cdots\theta_{n-1\,n}

\displaystyle\hskip 85.0pt\Big[\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(1)},\big[\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(2)},\cdots[\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(n-1)},\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(n)}]\cdots\big]\Big]\

\displaystyle\coloneq

\displaystyle\sum_{D}\frac{(-1)^{|D|}}{n^{2}\binom{n-1}{|D|}}\mathrm{CS}^{(n)}_{D}\,.

(2.15)

For the case of
n=4
, the grouping of permutations is shown in Table
1
.

. The final column shows the corresponding value of

).

For concreteness, focus on the set of permutations with
D=\{1\}
and
n=4
. Reading from the table, these are
2134,3124,4123
. Suppressing the integrations,

\mathrm{CS}^{\{1\}}_{4}=\theta_{12}\theta_{23}\theta_{34}\left([\mathcal{H}_{2},[\mathcal{H}_{1},[\mathcal{H}_{3},\mathcal{H}_{4}]]]+[\mathcal{H}_{3},[\mathcal{H}_{1},[\mathcal{H}_{2},\mathcal{H}_{4}]]]+[\mathcal{H}_{4},[\mathcal{H}_{1},[\mathcal{H}_{2},\mathcal{H}_{3}]]]\right).

(2.16)

Since the variables
x_{1},\dots,x_{4}
are integrated over, we are allowed to relabel them as we please. In particular, we can relabel them in such a way that at the end the term is proportional to the
1234
nested commutator,

\displaystyle\mathrm{CS}^{\{1\}}_{4}

\displaystyle\rightarrow\left(\theta_{21}\theta_{13}\theta_{34}+\theta_{23}\theta_{31}\theta_{14}+\theta_{23}\theta_{34}\theta_{41}\right)[\mathcal{H}_{1},[\mathcal{H}_{2},[\mathcal{H}_{3},\mathcal{H}_{4}]]]

\displaystyle=\theta_{21}\theta_{23}\theta_{34}[\mathcal{H}_{1},[\mathcal{H}_{2},[\mathcal{H}_{3},\mathcal{H}_{4}]]]\,,

(2.17)

where we have repeatedly used the
\theta
-function identities

\theta_{xa}\theta_{ab}+\theta_{xb}\theta_{ba}=\theta_{xa}\theta_{xb}\qquad\theta_{ab}\theta_{bx}+\theta_{ba}\theta_{ax}=\theta_{ax}\theta_{bx}\,.

(2.18)

This can be done for every descent set, and the results are tabulated in the final column of Table
1
above. Interestingly, we see that the final
\theta
-functions correspond to the original ordered
\theta_{12}\theta_{23}\theta_{34}
, with some of the
\theta
-functions flipped
\theta_{ij}\to\theta_{ji}
. The location of these flips exactly coincides with the values of the descent set,
in the sense that for
D=\{1,2\}
, the first and second
\theta
-functions are flipped, and so on.

We see this pattern appearing for any
n
, with explicit checks up to and including
n=8
. In general, if we sum over the set of permutations of
n
objects with descent set
D=\{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}\}
(and consequently with ascent set
A=\{j_{1},\dots,j_{(n-1)-k}\}
, such that
A\cup D=\{1,\dots,n{-}1\}
), then we find that

\Theta_{D}\coloneq\sum_{\sigma\in S^{D}_{n}}\sigma^{-1}(\theta_{12}\cdots\theta_{n{-}1\ n})=\left(\prod_{i\in D}\theta_{i{+}1\ i}\right)\left(\prod_{j\in A}\theta_{j\ j{+}1}\right)\,.

(2.19)

A proof of the identity above is given in Appendix
B
. The value of
\Theta_{D}
is tabulated in the last column of Table
1
. This means that we can rewrite the CS formula in the following new form:

\boxed{iN^{(n)}=\int\!d^{4}x_{1}\cdots d^{4}x_{n}\Big[\mathcal{H}_{1},\big[\mathcal{H}_{2},\cdots[\mathcal{H}_{n-1},\mathcal{H}_{n}]\cdots\big]\Big]\sum_{D\subseteq\{1,\dots,n-1\}}\frac{(-1)^{|D|}}{n^{2}\binom{n-1}{|D|}}\Theta_{D}}\ .

(2.20)

We now wish to comment on some features of this formula which,
to the best of our knowledge, has not been presented in the literature before.

1.
First, note that in the new formula only one particular ordering of nested commutators of Hamiltonians appears, namely
\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
.

2.
The sum to be performed is not over permutations, but over descent sets. Each descent set has a unique product of
\theta
-functions associated to it, given in
(
2.19
).

3.
We also note that (
2.20
) is a sum over
2^{n{-}1}
terms, which presents a computational improvement over the
n!
terms in the original CS formula (or the
(n{-}1)!
terms of the linearly independent version (
2.14
)).

While for small values of
n
, up to
n=4
, the compact formulae in (
2.9
) are shorter than (
2.20
), starting at
n=5
the expression found by
[
39
]
contains 22 terms, compared to the 16 coming from our new formula.

4.
Lastly, we can reduce the number of terms further by rewriting the sum in (
2.20
) in a different way. If we replace each
\theta_{i+1\,i}=1-\theta_{i\,i+1}
and collect like terms, we can replace the sum in
(
2.20
) by the following expression
[
44
]

\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n}\sum_{A\subseteq\{1,\dots,n{-}1\}}\frac{(-1)^{|A|}}{n-|A|}\tilde{\Theta}_{A}\,,\qquad\tilde{\Theta}_{A}\coloneq\prod_{j\in A}\theta_{j\,j{+}1}\,.

(2.21)

We have shown that our result (
2.20
)
agrees with (
2.21
) up to
n=15
. For example, for the
n=4
case, (
2.21
) reads

-\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{3}(\theta_{12}+\theta_{23}+\theta_{34})+\frac{1}{2}(\theta_{12}\theta_{23}+\theta_{12}\theta_{34}+\theta_{23}\theta_{34})-\theta_{12}\theta_{23}\theta_{34}\right)

(2.22)

While the sum produces
2^{n-1}
terms,
[
45
]
argues that due to the symmetries of the nested commutators in the integrand the number of non-zero terms when using (
2.21
) is
3\cdot 2^{n-3}
(in the case of
n=4
the vanishing terms are given by the term with no
\theta
-functions and
\theta_{12}
).

We wish to conclude this section with some intriguing observations on these new formulae.
Looking at the new formula (
2.20
), one particular term in the sum corresponding to
D=\{1,\dots,n-1\}
produces the combination of a chain of
\theta
-functions
\theta_{21}\theta_{32}\cdots\theta_{n\,n-1}
where position
x_{n}
is future-most. This is reminiscent of a causal response function, which also has nested commutators and a flow of time towards one point. In particular
[
46
]
,

R(\mathcal{H}_{n};\mathcal{H}_{n-1},\dots,\mathcal{H}_{1}){=}{\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n-1}}}\theta_{n\sigma(n-1)}\cdots\theta_{\sigma(3)\sigma(2)}\theta_{\sigma(2)\sigma(1)}[\dots[\mathcal{H}_{n},\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(n-1)}],\dots,\mathcal{H}_{\sigma(1)}]\,.

(2.23)

We can easily undo this sum over permutations by considering the
integrated
causal response function

\displaystyle\int\!d^{4}x_{1}

\displaystyle\cdots d^{4}x_{n}\ R(\mathcal{H}_{n};\mathcal{H}_{n-1},\dots,\mathcal{H}_{1})

\displaystyle=(-1)^{n-1}(n-1)!\int\!d^{4}x_{1}\cdots d^{4}x_{n}\ \theta_{21}\cdots\theta_{n\,n-1}[\mathcal{H}_{1},\dots,[\mathcal{H}_{n-1},\mathcal{H}_{n}]\dots]\,.

(2.24)

This causal response function is commonly computed by using the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, using a contour with a single time-fold

\displaystyle R(\mathcal{H}_{n};\mathcal{H}_{n-1},\dots,\mathcal{H}_{1})

(2.25)

where the dashed line indicates a difference between the Hamiltonian on fold I and fold II. One might wonder whether the other terms in the expression for the
N
-operator can be interpreted in this contour language. Extending the basic Schwinger-Keldysh contour as done in
[
47
]
, we can indeed express each term in (
2.21
) as a particular generalised contour. For example

n
n-1
\cdots
2
1
n

\displaystyle\rightarrow(-1)^{n-1}(n-2)!\ \theta_{23}\cdots\theta_{n{-}2\,n{-}1}\theta_{n{-}1\,n}[\mathcal{H}_{1},\dots,[\mathcal{H}_{n-1},\mathcal{H}_{n}]\dots]

(2.26)

omitting the integrations. Note that this is no longer an integrated response function, as the
\theta_{12}
term is missing; this is what necessitates an additional time-fold. This shift in perspective demonstrates that each term of (
2.21
) is Lorentz invariant despite containing
\theta
-functions, as each contour can be seen as an analytic continuation

[
48
,
49
]
of Euclidean correlators (Schwinger functions)
[
50
]
. As a whole, the Magnus expansion is therefore also term by term Lorentz invariant, implying that all the
\theta
-functions have to be combined into manifestly Lorentz-invariant objects. In Sections
4
and
5
we will demonstrate this explicitly through multiple examples.

3
Field commutators and propagators

Compared to the Dyson series, the Magnus series forgoes the time ordering in favour of imposing a fixed ordering among the
t_{i}
variables. Specifically, it features nested commutators of Hamiltonians instead of their time-ordered products.
As a consequence, when evaluating matrix elements of the
N
-operator we need to use a version of Wick’s theorem for products of fields, rather than time-ordered products.
The main relation, taking as an example the case of a single real scalar field
\phi
, is

\displaystyle\phi(x_{i})\phi(x_{j})=:\!\phi(x_{i})\phi(x_{j})\!:+\,\hbox to5.96pt{\vbox to8.89pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 2.97917pt\lower-4.44444pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}
{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-2.97917pt}{-2.5pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{}{{
{}{}{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}(x_{i})\hbox to5.96pt{\vbox to8.89pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 2.97917pt\lower-4.44444pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{

(3.3)

As usual in Wick’s theorem for time-ordered products, when dealing with products of normal-ordered operators, contractions between operators within the same normal-ordered product are excluded.

In the following, we introduce a number of functions we will need which describe commutators and anticommutators of two fields, as well as various Green’s functions. For the sake of completeness we now review these quantities in some detail.

3.1
Wightman commutation functions

We start with the standard mode expansion of a real, massive scalar field:

\displaystyle\begin{split}\phi(x)&=\phi^{(+)}(x)+\phi^{(-)}(x)=\int\frac{d^{3}p}{(2\pi)^{3}2E(\vec{p})}\Big[a(\vec{p})e^{-ip\cdot x}+a^{\dagger}(\vec{p})e^{ip\cdot x}\Big]\,,\,\end{split}

(3.4)

where the positive/negative frequency parts
\phi^{(\pm)}(x)
by definition contain the lowering/raising operators,
with

\displaystyle[a(\vec{p}),a^{\dagger}(\vec{q})]=(2\pi)^{3}2E(\vec{p})\delta^{(3)}(\vec{p}-\vec{q})\,.

(3.5)

The Wightman commutation function
\Delta^{(+)}(x)
that has appeared in (
3.2
) and the related one
\Delta^{(-)}(x)
are defined as
6
6

6

Our conventions are almost identical to those of Appendix C of Bjorken and Drell (BaD)
[
52
]
. We depart from theirs in that
\Delta^{(-)}_{\rm US}(x)=-\Delta^{(-)}_{\rm BaD}(x)
.

\displaystyle i\Delta^{(\pm)}_{ij}

\displaystyle=i\Delta^{(\pm)}(x_{i}-x_{j})\coloneqq[\phi^{(\pm)}(x_{i}),\phi^{(\mp)}(x_{j})]\,,

(3.6)

and satisfy

\displaystyle\Delta^{(\pm)}(-x)=-\Delta^{(\mp)}(x)\,.

(3.7)

Explicit expressions for
\Delta^{(\pm)}(x)
are

\displaystyle\begin{split}i\Delta^{(\pm)}(x)&=[\phi^{(\pm)}(x)\,,\,\phi^{(\mp)}(0)]\\
&=\pm\int\!\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}(2E(\vec{k}))}\,e^{\mp iE(\vec{k})x_{0}+i\vec{k}\cdot\vec{x}}\\
&=\pm\left.\int\!\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}(2E(\vec{k}))}\,e^{\mp ik\cdot x}\right|_{k_{0}=E(\vec{k})}\\
&=\pm\int\!\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,(2\pi)\delta(k^{2}-m^{2})\theta(\pm k_{0})\ ,\end{split}

(3.8)

where
E(\vec{k})\coloneq\sqrt{{\vec{k}}^{\,2}+m^{2}}
is the relativistic energy,
so that in momentum space the Wightman functions are

\displaystyle i\Delta^{(\pm)}(k)

\displaystyle=\pm(2\pi)\delta(k^{2}-m^{2})\theta(\pm k_{0})\,.

(3.9)

3.2
Pauli-Jordan and Hadamard functions

Next we introduce the commutator of two fields (also known as Pauli-Jordan function) as well as the anticommutator (sometimes called Hadamard function):

\displaystyle i\Delta_{ij}=i\Delta(x_{i}-x_{j})

\displaystyle\coloneqq[\phi(x_{i}),\phi(x_{j})]=i\Delta^{(+)}_{ij}+i\Delta^{(-)}_{ij}\,,

(3.10)

and

\displaystyle\Delta_{ij}^{(1)}=\Delta^{(1)}(x_{i}-x_{j})

\displaystyle\coloneqq\big\{\phi(x_{i}),\phi(x_{j})\big\}=i\Delta^{(+)}_{ij}-i\Delta^{(-)}_{ij}\,,

(3.11)

with

\displaystyle\Delta_{ji}=-\Delta_{ij}\,,\qquad\Delta^{(1)}_{ji}=\Delta^{(1)}_{ij}\,.

(3.12)

Note that
\Delta(x)
and
\Delta^{(1)}(x)
are even and odd solutions to the homogeneous Klein-Gordon equation,

\displaystyle\begin{split}(\Box+m^{2})\Delta(x)=(\Box+m^{2})\Delta^{(1)}(x)=0\,.\end{split}

(3.13)

We also quote the representations:

\displaystyle i\Delta(x)

\displaystyle=\int\!\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,(2\pi)\delta(k^{2}-m^{2})\,\text{sgn}(k_{0})\,,

(3.14)

\displaystyle\Delta^{(1)}(x)

\displaystyle=\int\!\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,(2\pi)\delta(k^{2}-m^{2})\,,

(3.15)

so that in momentum space the Pauli-Jordan and Hadamard functions are
7
7

7

As standard, we use the same symbol
\Delta
for propagators in position and momentum space.

\displaystyle i\Delta(k)

\displaystyle=(2\pi)\delta(k^{2}-m^{2})\,\text{sgn}(k_{0})\,,

(3.16)

\displaystyle\Delta^{(1)}(k)

\displaystyle=(2\pi)\delta(k^{2}-m^{2})\,,

(3.17)

where
\text{sgn}(k_{0})\coloneqq\theta(k_{0})-\theta(-k_{0})
is the sign of
k_{0}
.
Note that
\Delta^{(1)}(k)
is proportional to an on-shell delta function with no restriction on the sign of the energy. It is equal to twice a cut-propagator
\pi\,\delta(k^{2}-m^{2})
. Finally,
\Delta(x)
(unlike
\Delta^{(1)}(x)
) vanishes outside the lightcone,

\displaystyle\Delta(x)=0\quad\text{for}\quad x^{2}<0\,.

(3.18)

3.3
Propagators

The relevant Green functions are

\displaystyle i\Delta^{F}(x)

\displaystyle\coloneqq i\Delta^{(+)}(x)\theta(x_{0})-i\Delta^{(-)}(x)\theta(-x_{0})\,,

Feynman

(3.19)

\displaystyle i\Delta^{R}(x)

\displaystyle\coloneqq i\Delta(x)\theta(x_{0})\,,

Retarded

(3.20)

\displaystyle i\Delta^{A}(x)

\displaystyle\coloneqq-i\Delta(x)\theta(-x_{0})\,,

Advanced

(3.21)

\displaystyle i\Delta^{\bar{F}}(x)

\displaystyle\coloneqq i\Delta^{(-)}(x)\theta(x_{0})-i\Delta^{(+)}\theta(-x_{0})\,.

Anti-Feynman

(3.22)

Here
i\Delta^{\bar{F}}(x)
is the Green function obtained with anti time ordering, picking a contour that is the parity-reflected of the Feynman contour. Since
\Delta(x)=0

for
x^{2}<0
, i.e. outside the
lightcone, we see that the retarded and advanced propagators have support within the future and past
lightcone, respectively.
Note also the relations:

\displaystyle i\Delta^{F}(x)+i\Delta^{\bar{F}}(x)

\displaystyle=i\Delta^{R}(x)+i\Delta^{A}(x)\,,

(3.23)

\displaystyle i\Delta^{F}(x)-i\Delta^{\bar{F}}(x)

\displaystyle=\Delta^{(1)}(x)\,,

(3.24)

as well as

\displaystyle\Delta^{R}(-x)=\Delta^{A}(x)\,.

(3.25)

The connection between propagators and (anti-)time-ordered products is

\displaystyle i\Delta^{F}(x)

\displaystyle=\langle 0|T\big(\phi(x)\phi(0)\big)|0\rangle\,,

(3.26)

\displaystyle i\Delta^{\bar{F}}(x)

\displaystyle=-\langle 0|\bar{T}\big(\phi(x)\phi(0)\big)|0\rangle\,,

(3.27)

with

\displaystyle T\big(A(x)B(0)\big)

\displaystyle=\theta(x_{0})A(x)B(0)+\theta(-x_{0})B(0)A(x)\,,

(3.28)

\displaystyle\bar{T}\big(A(x)B(0)\big)

\displaystyle=\theta(x_{0})B(0)A(x)+\theta(-x_{0})A(x)B(0)\,.

(3.29)

In momentum space, the propagators are

\displaystyle i\Delta^{F}(k)

\displaystyle=\frac{i}{(k_{0}-E(\vec{k})+i\epsilon)(k_{0}+E(\vec{k})-i\epsilon)}=\frac{i}{k^{2}-m^{2}+i\epsilon}\,,

(3.30)

) and (

4
Tree-level amplitudes in the

\mathcal{H}_{I}=\frac{:\phi^{3}:}{3!}

theory

To describe the main ideas around the Magnus expansion, we focus on the theory of a real scalar field
\phi
of mass
m
with an interaction Hamiltonian

\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{I}=\frac{:\!\phi^{3}\!:}{3!}\,.

(4.1)

We omit the coupling factor in the interaction above to simplify later expressions.
The examples we will present below will suffice to illustrate the key features of the matrix elements of the

N
-operator introduced in (
2.8
), which we will refer to as Magnus amplitudes. This includes the emergence of retarded and advanced propagators, and the characteristic weights of the various diagrams. The latter will be related to certain Murua coefficients, as we will discuss in Section
6
.

4.1
The three-point amplitude

As a first simple example, we illustrate the three-point matrix element,
which we refer to as a Magnus amplitude:
8
8

8

For convenience in all matrix elements we include all the particles in the initial state, with all incoming momenta.

\displaystyle iN^{(1)}_{3}\coloneq\langle 0|iN^{(1)}|\phi(p_{1})\phi(p_{2})\phi(p_{3})\rangle\,,

(4.2)

where

\displaystyle iN^{(1)}

\displaystyle=-i\int\!d^{4}x\,\mathcal{H}_{I}(x)=-i\int\!d^{4}x\,\frac{:\phi^{3}:}{3!}

(4.3)

is the leading-order term in the Magnus expansion, and we defined
|\phi(p_{i})\rangle{\coloneq}a^{\dagger}(\vec{p}_{i})|0\rangle
.
The effect of contracting with external states is simply to produce

\displaystyle\frac{1}{3!}\langle 0|:\phi^{3}:|\phi(p_{1})\phi(p_{2})\phi(p_{3})\rangle=e^{-i(p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3})\cdot x}\,,

(4.4)

and, hence, the final matrix element is
9
9

9

We define
\hat{\delta}^{(n)}(p)\coloneq(2\pi)^{n}\delta^{(n)}(p)
.

\displaystyle iN_{3}^{(1)}=-i\int d^{4}x\,e^{-i(p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3})\cdot x}=-i\,\hat{\delta}^{(4)}(p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3})\,.

(4.5)

In this case, due to the absence of propagators there is no
difference to an ordinary
S
-matrix element.

4.2
The four-point amplitude

Our first non-trivial example is the four-point Magnus amplitude:

\displaystyle iN^{(2)}_{4}\coloneq\langle 0|iN^{(2)}|\phi(p_{1})\phi(p_{2})\phi(p_{3})\phi(p_{4})\rangle\,,

(4.6)

where

\displaystyle\begin{split}iN^{(2)}&=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,\theta(t_{1}-t_{2})\,\left[\mathcal{H}_{I}(x_{1}),\mathcal{H}_{I}(x_{2})\right]\,,\end{split}

(4.7)

is the second-order term in the Magnus expansion.
Performing Wick contractions using (
3.2
),
the relevant term in the commutator for computing the tree-level matrix element in (
4.6
) is

\displaystyle[\mathcal{H}_{I}(x_{1}),\mathcal{H}_{I}(x_{2})]

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(3!)^{2}}[:\phi_{1}^{3}:,:\phi_{2}^{3}:]\ni\frac{9}{(3!)^{2}}:\phi_{1}^{2}\hbox to5.96pt{\vbox to8.89pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 2.97917pt\lower-4.44444pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{}{{

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-2.97917pt}{-2.5pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

\lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{}{{

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2!)^{2}}(i\Delta_{12}^{(+)}):\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}:-(x_{1}\leftrightarrow x_{2})=\frac{1}{(2!)^{2}}(i\Delta_{12}^{(+)}-i\Delta_{21}^{(+)}):\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}:\,

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2!)^{2}}(i\Delta_{12}):\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}:\,,

(4.8)

where we recall that
\Delta_{12}\coloneq\Delta^{(+)}_{12}+\Delta^{(-)}_{12}=\Delta^{(+)}_{12}-\Delta^{(+)}_{21}
is the commutation function.
Other possible Wick contractions will not contribute when we contract with external states.
We can also obtain this result using

\displaystyle[\phi_{1}^{3},\phi_{2}^{3}]

\displaystyle=\phi_{1}^{2}[\phi_{1},\phi_{2}^{3}]+\phi_{1}[\phi_{1},\phi_{2}^{3}]\phi_{1}+[\phi_{1},\phi_{2}^{3}]\phi_{1}^{2}\,,

(4.9a)

\displaystyle[\phi_{1},\phi_{2}^{3}]

\displaystyle=[\phi_{1},\phi_{2}]\phi_{2}^{2}+\phi_{2}[\phi_{1},\phi_{2}]\phi_{2}+\phi_{2}^{2}[\phi_{1},\phi_{2}]=3i\Delta_{12}\phi_{2}^{2}\,,

(4.9b)

which together imply that

\displaystyle\frac{1}{(3!)^{2}}[\phi_{1}^{3},\phi_{2}^{3}]=\frac{1}{3\cdot(2!)^{2}}i\Delta_{12}(\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}+\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{1}+\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{1}^{2})\,.

(4.10)

Upon applying normal ordering this matches (
4.2
).
In this second approach, the function
i\Delta_{12}
appears almost immediately,
and further multiplying it by
\theta_{12}
gives rise to a retarded propagator
i\Delta^{R}_{12}
.
Ultimately,

\displaystyle iN^{(2)}

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,(i\Delta^{R}_{12})\left(\frac{1}{(2!)^{2}}:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}:+\cdots\right)\,,

(4.11)

is the relevant term in the Magnus series.
The dots indicate the remaining Wick contractions
which do not enter the tree-level Magnus amplitude and that are therefore omitted.
Crucially, we have now absorbed all factors of
\theta_{ij}
to obtain a result
that is manifestly Lorentz invariant.

We may then consider the effect of contractions on external states. These give

\displaystyle\frac{1}{(2!)^{2}}\langle 0|:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}:|\phi(p_{1})\phi(p_{2})\phi(p_{3})\phi(p_{4})\rangle=E(x_{1},x_{2})+E(x_{2},x_{1})\,,

(4.12)

where

E(x_{1},x_{2})=e^{-i(p_{1}+p_{2})\cdot x_{1}-i(p_{3}+p_{4})\cdot x_{2}}+e^{-i(p_{2}+p_{3})\cdot x_{1}-i(p_{4}+p_{1})\cdot x_{2}}+e^{-i(p_{1}+p_{3})\cdot x_{1}-i(p_{4}+p_{2})\cdot x_{2}}.

(4.13)

The full tree-level Magnus amplitude then becomes

\displaystyle\begin{split}iN^{(2)}_{4}&=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,(i\Delta^{R}_{12})\Big[E(x_{1},x_{2})+E(x_{2},x_{1})\Big]\\
&=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,(i\Delta^{R}_{12}+i\Delta^{A}_{12})E(x_{1},x_{2})\,.\end{split}

(4.14)

where in the second line we have applied the interchange symmetry
x_{1}\leftrightarrow x_{2}
.
Fourier transforming yields

\displaystyle iN^{(2)}_{4}

\displaystyle=\hat{\delta}^{(4)}(p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3}+p_{4})\,\mathcal{M}\,,

(4.15)

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}\left[(i\Delta^{R}{+}i\Delta^{A})(p_{1}{+}p_{2})+(i\Delta^{R}{+}i\Delta^{A})(p_{2}{+}p_{3})+(i\Delta^{R}{+}i\Delta^{A})(p_{1}{+}p_{3})\right]\,.

Graphically, we can represent (
4.15
) as

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}=

\displaystyle\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}\Biggl(\hbox to100.81pt{\vbox to52.53pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 36.17848pt\lower-26.26465pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces {}{{}}{}
{}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L -27.84 27.84}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}{}}}{{}{}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-32.84547pt}{19.05667pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
{}{{}}{}
{}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L -27.84 -27.84}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}{}}}{{}{}}

(4.16)

where the direction of the arrow indicates the direction of causality flow.

Two observations are in order here:

1.
First, anticipating a point we will make later, we notice that the factor of
1/2
in (
4.2
) corresponds precisely to the Murua coefficient which will be introduced
in (
6.3b
).

2.
We also note that at tree level the four-point Magnus amplitude is obtained by writing the same Feynman diagrams as for the standard amplitude, except for the replacement

\displaystyle i\Delta^{F}(p)\longrightarrow\frac{1}{2}\big(i\Delta^{R}+i\Delta^{A}\big)(p)\,.

(4.17)

One may also note that

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\big(i\Delta^{R}(p)+i\Delta^{A}(p)\big)=i\Delta^{F}(p)-\frac{1}{2}\Delta^{(1)}(p)\,,

(4.18)

where

\displaystyle\Delta^{(1)}(p)\coloneq i\Delta^{(+)}(p)-i\Delta^{(-)}(p)=(2\pi)\delta(p^{2}-m^{2})\,,

(4.19)

is the Hadamard function introduced in (
3.15
). The latter function has support only on shell, and hence in general it will not contribute at tree level for generic kinematics.

4.3
The five-point amplitude

Next we compute the five-point Magnus amplitude:

\displaystyle iN_{5}^{(3)}=\langle 0|iN^{(3)}|\phi(p_{1})\cdots\phi(p_{5})\rangle\,,

(4.20)

where

\displaystyle iN^{(3)}=\frac{(-i)^{3}}{6}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}\ \theta_{12}\ \theta_{23}\ \left([\mathcal{H}_{1},[\mathcal{H}_{2},\mathcal{H}_{3}]]+[\mathcal{H}_{3},[\mathcal{H}_{2},\mathcal{H}_{1}]]\right)\,.

(4.21)

As usual,
\mathcal{H}_{i}
stands for
\mathcal{H}(x_{i})
and
\theta_{ij}\coloneq\theta(t_{i}-t_{j})
. A short computation shows that
10
10

10

One may arrive at different-looking but in fact identical expressions for commutators due to the commutator of two fields being equal to a c-number. For instance,

[\phi_{1}^{3},\phi_{2}^{3}]=3i\Delta_{12}(\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}+\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{1}^{2}+\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{1})
, and
[\phi_{1}^{3},\phi_{2}^{3}]=3i\Delta_{12}(\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}+\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{1}^{2}+\phi_{2}\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2})
. Both expressions are correct since
\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{1}-\phi_{2}\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}=[\phi_{1},\phi_{2}]\phi_{2}\phi_{1}-\phi_{2}\phi_{1}[\phi_{1},\phi_{2}]=0
, since
[\phi_{1},\phi_{2}]
is a c-number.

\displaystyle[\mathcal{H}_{1},[\mathcal{H}_{2},\mathcal{H}_{3}]]

\displaystyle=\frac{9}{(3!)^{3}}(i\Delta_{23})

(4.22)

\displaystyle\Big[

\displaystyle(i\Delta_{12})\big(\phi_{2}\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}+\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2}+\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{1}^{2}+\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}+\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{2}+\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{1}^{2}\big)

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle(i\Delta_{13})\big(\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{1}^{2}+\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{3}+\phi_{3}\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}+\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{2}^{2}+\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}+\phi_{2}\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{2}\big)\Big]\,.

We will set
N^{(3)}\coloneq N_{123}+N_{321}
, where the two terms denote the contributions arising from the two orderings of the nested commutators in (
4.21
).
We then find
11
11

11

Note that we can rewrite
\theta_{12}\theta_{23}=\theta_{12}\theta_{23}\theta_{13}
.

\displaystyle iN_{123}

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{3}}{6}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}\ (i\Delta^{R}_{23})\frac{1}{(2!)^{2}}\Big[(i\Delta^{R}_{12}):\!\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\!:+\theta_{12}(i\Delta^{R}_{13}):\!\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\!:\Big]

\displaystyle\qquad+\cdots\,,

(4.23)

again ignoring further field contractions that will not contribute to the tree-level amplitude.

We note that in (
4.3
) there is an additional
\theta_{12}
which,
at first glance, is not associated with a retarded or advanced propagator.
In order to achieve manifest Lorentz invariance it is necessary for us to absorb it.
This is not difficult though:
since
\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{13}:\!\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\!:
is symmetric under the exchange
x_{1}\leftrightarrow x_{2}
, we can rewrite (
4.3
) without the
\theta
-function as
12
12

12

Similar manipulations led Dyson to the introduction of time-ordered products
[
1
]
.

\displaystyle iN_{123}

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{3}}{6}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}\ (i\Delta^{R}_{23})\frac{1}{(2!)^{2}}\Big[(i\Delta^{R}_{12}):\!\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\!:+\frac{1}{2}(i\Delta^{R}_{13}):\!\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\!:\Big]

\displaystyle\qquad+\cdots\,.

(4.24)

The relative factor
1/2
between the two terms in the above result is our first example of different weights associated to different routings of advanced and retarded propagators.

We can also describe this simplification diagrammatically. If we represent the points
x_{1,2,3}
as the vertices of a graph, we can interpret the retarded propagators as directed edges between vertices. We then represent the leftover
\theta
-functions as additional (red) directed edges. We use the arrows to represent the flow of
time, so that if an edge goes from
j
to
i
then
t_{i}>t_{j}
, and we introduce the notation

Our notation for the final graph in (

) and similar ones is inspired by

.

We can understand this as follows: the term in (
4.26
) has support in the integration subregion
t_{1}>t_{2}>t_{3}
, as shown by the arrow orientations. But the product of retarded propagators
(i\Delta^{R}_{23})\,(i\Delta^{R}_{13})
alone allows for a bigger region, namely
t_{1}>t_{3}\,,\,t_{2}>t_{3}
. The latter contains one more subregion,
t_{2}>t_{1}>t_{3}
, but this can be obtained via symmetrising
x_{1}\leftrightarrow x_{2}
in (
4.27
). Adding both subregions we recover the full
t_{1}>t_{3}\,,\,t_{2}>t_{3}
region, and therefore the result is given just in terms of retarded propagators.

The same strategy can be applied to
N_{321}
, with the result,

\displaystyle iN_{321}

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{3}}{6}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}\ \frac{1}{(2!)^{2}}(i\Delta^{R}_{12})\Big[(i\Delta^{R}_{23}):\!\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\!:+\frac{1}{2}(i\Delta^{R}_{13}):\!\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\!:\Big]

\displaystyle\qquad+\cdots\,.

{{}}
}
\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }
{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\ \right].\end{split}

(4.33)

Note that the position of the external legs in the graphs is encoded in the exponential in (
4.32
). Moreover, we have omitted the labels of external lines in (
4.33
) for notational simplicity, but they are to be summed over all possible permutations
\sigma\in S_{5}
of
(p_{1},p_{2},p_{3},p_{4},p_{5})
. Before concluding this section, two observations are in order.

1.
The factors inside the square brackets correspond precisely to the Murua coefficients found in (
6.3c
). The factor of
1/8
outside is to compensate for overcounting in the sum over all permutations.

2.
In the four-point example, we saw that the single
\theta
-function in the Magnus expansion immediately combined with a
\Delta
function to produce retarded and advanced propagators. In the five-point case, the Magnus expansion (
4.21
) contains two
\theta
-functions, only one of which initially combines with a
\Delta
function; nevertheless, we showed that the second
\theta
-function can also be eliminated, as in (
3.25
). This behaviour is a general feature of the expansion, although it becomes increasingly challenging to identify the rearrangements needed to remove all remaining
\theta
-functions. The forthcoming six-point example will be particularly instructive in this regard (and also to confirm the pattern of the appearance of Murua coefficients, discussed in more detail in Section
6.1
).

4.4
The six-point amplitude

As a final example at tree level, we now focus on the six-point Magnus amplitude

\displaystyle N_{6}^{(4)}=\langle 0|N^{(4)}|\phi(p_{1})\cdots\phi(p_{6})\rangle\,,

(4.34)

where
N^{(4)}
was defined in (
2.9d
).
For convenience we define

iN^{(4)}_{ijkl}:=\frac{(-i)^{4}}{12}\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}d^{4}x_{4}\ \theta_{12}\theta_{23}\theta_{34}[\mathcal{H}_{i},[\mathcal{H}_{j},[\mathcal{H}_{k},\mathcal{H}_{l}]]]\,,

(4.35)

so that

\displaystyle N^{(4)}=N^{(4)}_{1234}+N^{(4)}_{4312}+N^{(4)}_{2341}+N^{(4)}_{1432}\,,

(4.36)

and treat the nested commutators separately.
Starting from
N^{(4)}_{1234}
,
we find that

\displaystyle\begin{split}iN^{(4)}_{1234}:=&\frac{-i}{12}\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}d^{4}x_{4}\ \left[\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{12}\theta_{23}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}\right.\\
&+(\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{12}+\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{12}\theta_{23})\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}:}{(2!)^{2}}\\
&+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{23}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}:}{(2!)^{2}}+\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{12}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}\\
&\left.+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{2}}\right]+\cdots\,,\end{split}

(4.37)

again ignoring further contractions from Wick’s theorem that will not contribute to the tree-level amplitude.
Our task is now to eliminate the leftover
\theta
-functions.

We start with the first term in (
4.37
) and symmetrise:

\displaystyle\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{12}\theta_{23}:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}:\to

\displaystyle\frac{1}{3!}\big(\theta_{12}\theta_{23}+\theta_{23}\theta_{31}+\theta_{31}\theta_{12}+\theta_{13}\theta_{32}+\theta_{32}\theta_{21}+\theta_{21}\theta_{13}\big)

\displaystyle\times\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}:

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{3!}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}:.

(4.38)

We can understand this as follows:
N_{1234}^{(4)}
contains an ordering
t_{1}{>}t_{2}{>}t_{3}{>}t_{4}
,
but the retarded propagators only imply
t_{1,2,3}>t_{4}
. The latter region can be divided in six sub-regions
t_{\sigma(1)}>t_{\sigma(2)}>t_{\sigma(3)}>t_{4}
, where
\sigma
are all permutations of three indices and only the region
\sigma(i)=i
appears in (
4.37
). However, since
t_{1,2,3}
are integration variables, we can fully symmetrise them to recover all six regions. Diagrammatically,
16
16

16

This notation reintroduces a factor of
i
per propagator compared to (
4.4
).

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\,,

(4.39)

the
1/3!
manifesting naturally as a symmetry factor.

Then, we consider the next three terms in (
4.37
), namely

\displaystyle 2(\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{12}+\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{12}\theta_{23}):\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}:+2\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{23}:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}:

\displaystyle\to 2\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}(\theta_{12}+\theta_{21}\theta_{13}+\theta_{31}):\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}:

\displaystyle\qquad=2\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}:\,,

(4.40)

where the arrow means that the equality holds upon integration.
All three terms have the same retarded propagators, up to relabelling of the integration variables
t_{i}
that we have performed above. More explicitly: we have relabelled
\{t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},t_{4}\}\to\{t_{2},t_{1},t_{3},t_{4}\}
and
\{t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},t_{4}\}\to\{t_{2},t_{3},t_{1},t_{4}\}
, in the second and third term respectively, thus obtaining a common factor
\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}
.

(4.43)

With all
\theta
-functions in (
4.37
) now absorbed, we have

\displaystyle iN^{(4)}_{1234}:=

\displaystyle\frac{-i}{12}\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}d^{4}x_{4}\ \left[\frac{1}{6}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}\right.

\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}+\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}:}{(2!)^{2}}

\displaystyle\left.+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{2}}\right]+\cdots\,.

(4.44)

The last term, which we can depict as

,
is proportional to
\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}

and does not require further simplifications.

Then we move onto the nested commutator
N^{(4)}_{4312}
and we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}iN^{(4)}_{4312}:=&\frac{-i}{12}\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}d^{4}x_{4}\ \left[\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{14}\theta_{23}\theta_{34}\frac{:\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}\right.\\
&+(\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\theta_{34}+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{24}\theta_{23}\theta_{34})\frac{:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{2}}\\
&+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{23}\frac{:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{2}}+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{24}\theta_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}\\
&\left.+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{2}}\right]\,.\end{split}

(4.45)

The first term gives

\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{14}\theta_{23}\theta_{34}:\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:=\frac{1}{6}\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{14}:\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:\,,

(4.51)

Now all theta functions have disappeared, and we get

\displaystyle iN^{(4)}_{4312}:=

\displaystyle\frac{-i}{12}\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}d^{4}x_{4}\ \left[\frac{1}{6}\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{14}\frac{:\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}+\frac{1}{2}\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{24}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}\right.

\displaystyle\left.+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\frac{:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{2}}+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{2}}\right].

(4.52)

Finally we consider the last two nested commutators
N^{(4)}_{2341}
and
N^{(4)}_{1432}
. In this case, as we are about to show, we need both of them to eliminate all theta functions
\theta_{ij}
. We have

\displaystyle\begin{split}i&N^{(4)}_{2341}+iN^{(4)}_{1432}=\frac{-i}{12}\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}d^{4}x_{4}\ \left[-\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{12}\theta_{23}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}\right.\\
&+\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{12}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{24}\theta_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}-\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{14}\theta_{23}\theta_{34}\frac{:\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}\\
&+(\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{23}{+}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\theta_{12}\theta_{23}\theta_{34})\frac{:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}:}{(2!)^{2}}+\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\theta_{12}\theta_{34}\frac{{:}\,\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}^{2}\,{:}}{(2!)^{2}}\\
&\left.+(\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}+\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{24}\theta_{12}\theta_{34})\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{2}}+\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{24}\theta_{12}\theta_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}:}{(2!)^{2}}\right].\end{split}

(4.53)

Some propagator terms above have a permutation symmetry, such as
\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}
which is symmetric in
\{1,2,3\}
or
\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}
which is symmetric in
\{1,2\}
. Simplifying the
\theta
-functions in these terms is straightforward and follows the same reasoning as before, using the identities (
4.4
), (
4.43
), (
4.4
), and (
4.51
).
Besides them, there are five leftover terms that simplify together as follows,

\displaystyle\begin{split}&2\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{34}\theta_{23}:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}:+2\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\theta_{12}\theta_{23}\theta_{34}:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}:\\
&+2\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{24}\theta_{12}\theta_{34}:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}^{2}:+2\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{24}\theta_{12}\theta_{34}:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}:\\
&+2\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{23}\theta_{12}\theta_{34}:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}^{2}:\\
&\rightarrow 2\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{34}\big(\theta_{23}+\theta_{13}\theta_{32}\theta_{24}+\theta_{31}\theta_{42}+\theta_{31}\theta_{24}+\theta_{13}\theta_{42}\big):\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}:\\
&=2\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{34}:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}:,\end{split}

(4.54)

using the identity

\hbox to325.47pt{\vbox to28.14pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\;\lower-24.73956pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\par{}{{}}{}

{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\,.

(4.55)

Note that to identify each of the five subregions we had to first relabel terms to find a common propagator structure, just like we did in (
4.4
). Also note that some of the five terms above come from
N^{(4)}_{2341}
and some from
N^{(4)}_{1432}
, meaning that we need to consider the sum to see the simplification of theta functions.

Putting everything together, we get

\displaystyle iN^{(4)}_{2341}+iN^{(4)}_{1432}=\frac{-i}{12}\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}d^{4}x_{4}\ \left[-\frac{1}{6}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}\right.

\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}+\frac{1}{2}\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{24}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}-\frac{1}{6}\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{14}\frac{:\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}

\displaystyle\left.+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}\phi_{4}:}{(2!)^{2}}+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}^{2}:}{(2!)^{2}}\right].

(4.56)

Note that the terms
\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{34}
and
\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{13}\Delta^{R}_{14}
appear with coefficient
-1/6
here, but they appear with coefficient
+1/6
in
N^{(4)}_{1234}
and
N^{(4)}_{4312}
and hence they drop out.

Overall, the complete expression for the fourth-order
N
-operator is

\displaystyle iN^{(4)}

\displaystyle=\frac{-i}{12}\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}d^{4}x_{4}\ \left[(\Delta^{R}_{34}\Delta^{R}_{41}\Delta^{R}_{42}+\Delta^{R}_{14}\Delta^{R}_{24}\Delta^{R}_{43})\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}\phi_{3}^{2}:}{(2!)^{3}}\right.

(4.57)

\displaystyle\left.+(3\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{23}\Delta^{R}_{34}+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{32}\Delta^{R}_{34}+\Delta^{R}_{21}\Delta^{R}_{32}\Delta^{R}_{34}+\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{R}_{32}\Delta^{R}_{43})\frac{:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}^{2}}{(2!)^{2}}:\right]+\cdots.

Sandwiching this between the states as in (
4.34
), we arrive at the six-point Magnus amplitude

\displaystyle iN^{(4)}_{6}

\displaystyle=(-i)^{4}\hat{\delta}^{(4)}(p_{1}+\cdots+p_{6})\,\mathcal{M}^{(4)}_{6}\,,

(4.58)

(4.59)

As before, we have omitted the labels of external lines for notational simplicity, but they are to be summed over all possible permutations
\sigma\in S_{6}
of
(p_{1},p_{2},p_{3},p_{4},p_{5},p_{6})
. Also, the coefficients in front of each diagram (ignoring the coefficients outside the sum, which are due to overcounting) correspond to the Murua coefficients in (
6.3d
). In particular, notice the absence of two star diagrams with all arrows incoming/outgoing, which indeed have vanishing Murua coefficient.

Finally, the subtle recombination of

\theta
-functions into manifestly Lorentz-invariant retarded and advanced propagators that we have illustrated so far in several examples is actually general, as argued in Section
2.2
.

5
One-loop amplitudes in the

\mathcal{H}_{I}=\frac{:\phi^{3}:}{3!}

theory

Still working in our theory of a real scalar of mass
m
with a cubic interaction, we now show a few examples of one-loop amplitudes. These will highlight intriguing connections to the tree amplitudes computed in the previous section, which we will further investigate and explain in Section
7.2
.

5.1
The bubble

As a first one-loop example, we consider the two-point matrix element

N^{(2)}_{2}=\langle 0|N^{(2)}|\phi(p_{1})\phi(p_{2})\rangle\,,

(5.1)

where
N^{(2)}
is the second-order term in the Magnus expansion given in (
4.7
),
that is

\displaystyle iN^{(2)}_{2}=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3!}\right)^{2}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,\theta(t_{1}-t_{2})\langle 0|[:\phi^{3}(x_{1}):,:\phi^{3}(x_{2}):]|\phi(p_{1})\phi(p_{2})\rangle\,.

(5.2)

We can work out directly the commutator
[{:\phi^{3}(x_{1}):},{:\phi^{3}(x_{2}):}]
. We do it first
without normal ordering which we reinstate at the end.
In order to do, so we first recall (
4.10
), and then note that in order to
get the one-loop bubble we need to perform one more Wick contraction.
This leads to

\displaystyle\begin{split}[\phi_{1}^{3},\phi_{2}^{3}]&\rightarrow 3i\Delta_{12}\Big(2\cdot 2:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}:i\Delta^{(+)}_{12}+2:\phi_{2}\phi_{1}:i\Delta^{(+)}_{12}\\
&+2:\phi_{2}\phi_{1}:i\Delta^{(+)}_{21}+2\cdot 2:\phi_{2}\phi_{1}:i\Delta^{(+)}_{21}\Big)\\
&=3i\Delta_{12}\cdot 6:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}:\Big(i\Delta_{12}^{(+)}+i\Delta_{21}^{(+)}\Big)\\
&=18\,i\Delta_{12}\Delta^{(1)}_{12}:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}:\,.\end{split}

(5.3)

We can extend the tree-level diagrammatic notation in (
4.25
) to include now the Hadamard function
\Delta^{(1)}_{ij}
introduced in (
3.15
):

For

we can now write

\displaystyle\begin{split}iN^{(2)}&=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3!}\right)^{2}\cdot 18\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,\big(\theta_{12}i\Delta_{12}\big)\,\Delta^{(1)}_{12}\,:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}:+\dots\\
&=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{4}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,\big(i\Delta^{R}_{12}\big)\,\Delta^{(1)}_{12}\,:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}:+\dots\,,\end{split}

(5.6)

where the terms omitted do not contribute to the matrix element
N^{(2)}_{2}
. Note that as usual we have symmetrised in
x_{1}\leftrightarrow x_{2}
to get rid of
\theta
functions.
We then use that

\displaystyle\langle 0|:\phi(x_{1})\phi(x_{2}):|\phi(p_{1})\phi(p_{2})\rangle=e^{-i(p_{1}\cdot x_{1}+p_{2}\cdot x_{2})}+e^{-i(p_{1}\cdot x_{2}+p_{2}\cdot x_{1})}\,,

(5.7)

to get

\displaystyle\begin{split}iN_{2}^{(2)}&=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{4}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,\big(i\Delta^{R}_{12}\big)\,\Delta^{(1)}_{12}\,(e^{-i(p_{1}\cdot x_{1}+p_{2}\cdot x_{2})}+e^{-i(p_{1}\cdot x_{2}+p_{2}\cdot x_{1})})\\
&=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{4}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,e^{-i(p_{1}{\cdot}x_{1}+p_{2}{\cdot}x_{2})}\Big(i\Delta^{R}_{12}\Delta^{(1)}_{12}+i\Delta^{R}_{21}\Delta^{(1)}_{21}\Big)\\
&=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{4}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,e^{-i(p_{1}{\cdot}x_{1}+p_{2}{\cdot}x_{2})}\,\Delta^{(1)}_{12}\Big(i\Delta^{R}_{12}+i\Delta^{A}_{12}\Big)\,.\end{split}

(5.8)

In this derivation we have used that
i\Delta^{R}(x)=\theta(x_{0})i\Delta(x)
, and changed integration variables
x_{1}\leftrightarrow x_{2}
in the term containing
e^{-i(p_{1}\cdot x_{2}+p_{2}\cdot x_{1})}
.
Thus we conclude that

\displaystyle\begin{split}iN_{2}^{(2)}&=\frac{(-i)^{2}}{4}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,e^{-i(p_{1}{\cdot}x_{1}+p_{2}{\cdot}x_{2})}\,\Delta^{(1)}_{12}\Big(i\Delta^{R}_{12}+i\Delta^{A}_{12}\Big)\,,\end{split}

(5.9)

that is,

(5.10)

Three important comments are in order here.

1.
First, a key feature of (
5.1
) and (
5.6
) is that they are cut integrals, since
\Delta^{(1)}(q)=(2\pi)\,\delta(q^{2}-m^{2})
. Consequently, we are effectively performing phase-space integrals over a tree-level quantity. Note that this representation differs from the Feynman-tree-theorem representation of the
T
-matrix
[
32
,
33
]
(since there one has to sum over multiple cuts as well) and the
Q
-cuts of
[
38
]
.

2.
Furthermore, and importantly, we will see that for a one-loop
n
-point Magnus amplitude, what we are actually integrating is an
(n+2)
-point tree-level Magnus amplitude, where by this we mean the sum of all the tree-level Magnus diagrams at
n+2
points.
This correspondence is already manifest by comparing (
5.6
) to (
4.11
).
In fact, we can go from the first to the second by simply performing the replacement

\displaystyle:\phi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}:\to 2\Delta^{(1)}_{12}:\phi_{1}\phi_{2}:\,.

(5.11)

We will see a similar relation between the five-point tree amplitude and the one-loop triangle later in Section
5.2
,
and will discuss this further in Sections
7.1.2
and
7.2
.

3.
Furthermore, it is instructive to perform a comparison with the Dyson series.
The difference between Magnus and Dyson matrix elements for the process at hand is:

\displaystyle iN^{(2)}_{2}-iT^{(2)}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot\int d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,e^{-i(p_{1}\cdot x_{1}+p_{2}\cdot x_{2})}\left[(i\Delta_{12}^{(+)})^{2}+(i\Delta_{12}^{(-)})^{2}\right]\,.

(5.12)

This precisely corresponds to the expected relation
[
4
]

\displaystyle iN^{(2)}=iT^{(2)}+\frac{1}{2}T^{(1)}T^{(1)}\,,

(5.13)

between Magnus and
T
-matrix elements, since
17
17

17

The factor of
1/2
in (
5.14
) arises due to the presence of identical particles.

\displaystyle\langle 0|T^{(1)}T^{(1)}|\phi(p_{1})\phi(p_{2})\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}\,e^{-i(p_{1}\cdot x_{1}+p_{2}\cdot x_{2})}\left[(i\Delta_{12}^{(+)})^{2}+(i\Delta_{12}^{(-)})^{2}\right]\,.

(5.14)

4.
Finally, let us evaluate directly (
5.1
), which can be done conveniently using
(
3.23
) and (
3.24
). We find the result

\displaystyle iN_{2}^{(2)}

\displaystyle=\hat{\delta}^{(4)}(p_{1}+p_{2})\frac{(-i)^{2}}{4}\int\!\frac{d^{4}q}{(2\pi)^{4}}\left[i\Delta^{F}(q)i\Delta^{F}(q-p_{1})-i\Delta^{\bar{F}}(q)i\Delta^{\bar{F}}(q-p_{1})\right]\,,

(5.15)

which is nothing but the difference of the bubble integral evaluated with the Feynman prescription and the same integral but with an anti-Feynman prescription. To be more concrete let us assume that the internal particles are massless and the external momenta
p_{1,2}
are off-shell.
Using well-known results for the bubble integrals
we find

\displaystyle\begin{split}iN_{2}^{(2)}&=\hat{\delta}^{(4)}(p_{1}+p_{2})\frac{c_{\Gamma}}{4\epsilon(1-2\epsilon)}\left[-i\,(-s-i\varepsilon)^{-\epsilon}-\text{c.c.}\right]\\
&=\hat{\delta}^{(4)}(p_{1}+p_{2})\frac{(-i\,c_{\Gamma})}{4\epsilon(1-2\epsilon)}\left[(-s-i\varepsilon)^{-\epsilon}+(-s+i\varepsilon)^{-\epsilon}\right]\\
&=\hat{\delta}^{(4)}(p_{1}+p_{2})\frac{(-i\,c_{\Gamma})}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}+\log(|s|)+2\right)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\,,\end{split}

(5.16)

where
s=p_{1}^{2}
and
c_{\Gamma}=\Gamma(1+\epsilon)\Gamma^{2}(1-\epsilon)/(\Gamma(1-2\epsilon)(4\pi)^{2-\epsilon})
.
This means that in this one-loop Magnus matrix element the real part/discontinuity of the
T
-matrix element has been removed. Notice that this removal is achieved due to the last term in (
5.13
).

5.2
The three-point triangle and bubble topologies

We now compute the Magnus matrix element

\displaystyle N_{3}^{(3)}=\langle 0|N^{(3)}|\phi(p_{1})\phi(p_{2})\phi(p_{3})\rangle\,,

(5.17)

where
N^{(3)}
is given in (
4.21
).
Note that the operator
N^{(3)}
contains two types of terms contributing to the matrix element
N_{3}^{(3)}
, which give rise to two different graph topologies, namely

N^{(3)}\big|_{\rm tri}\propto\,:\!\phi(p_{1})\phi(p_{2})\phi(p_{3})\!:\,,\qquad N^{(3)}\big|_{\rm bub}\propto\,:\!\phi(p_{i})^{2}\phi(p_{j})\!:\,,

(5.18)

where
N^{(3)}\big|_{\rm tri}
will give rise to one-loop triangle graphs and
N^{(3)}\big|_{\rm bub}
will give rise to one-loop three-point graphs with a bubble on an external leg. For simplicity, we will focus on the former case and only quote the final result for the latter.

For convenience, similarly to Section
4.3
, we set

\displaystyle N^{(3)}\big|_{\rm tri}=N_{123}^{(3)}\big|_{\rm tri}+N_{321}^{(3)}\big|_{\rm tri}\,,

(5.19)

where the two terms correspond to the contributions in
N^{(3)}\big|_{\rm tri}
arising from the two distinct commutators, respectively.
We then find, using the result (
4.22
), performing one more Wick contraction and then normal-ordering the rest,

\displaystyle\begin{split}&iN_{123}^{(3)}\big|_{\rm tri}=\frac{(-i)^{3}}{6}\left(\frac{1}{3!}\right)^{3}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}\ :\!\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\!:\\
&3\cdot 36(i\Delta^{R}_{23})\Big[(i\Delta^{R}_{12})\Delta^{(1)}_{13}+(i\Delta^{R}_{13})(\theta_{12}\Delta^{(1)}_{12})\Big]\,\,,\end{split}

(5.20)

where since
\Delta_{13}^{R}\Delta_{23}^{R}\Delta^{(1)}_{12}:\!\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\!:
is symmetric under the exchange
x_{1}\leftrightarrow x_{2}
,
N_{123}^{(3)}\big|_{\rm tri}
can be rewritten as

\displaystyle\begin{split}&iN_{3,123}^{(3)}\big|_{\rm tri}=\frac{(-i)^{3}}{12}\int\!d^{4}x_{1}d^{4}x_{2}d^{4}x_{3}\ :\!\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\!:\\
&(i\Delta^{R}_{23})\Big[(i\Delta^{R}_{12})\Delta^{(1)}_{13}+\frac{1}{2}(i\Delta^{R}_{13})\Delta^{(1)}_{12}\Big]\,\,.\end{split}

(5.21)

Diagrammatically, the cancellation of the
\theta
-functions happens in the same way as before,
